title: Nobel Prize 2026 roundup: Honorees include optogenetics, neutrino, and chirality researchers/

By Yifei Zhu and Maxwell Wright

Physiology or Medicine

This award was given to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel for their contribution to optogenetics, a biological technique that combines genetic engineering and optics to control and monitor the activity of individual cells — most commonly neurons — with millisecond-scale precision using light.

They discovered that, when blue light illuminated the special protein channelrhodopsin, charged ions would flow into the cell, creating an electrical impulse. Whichever cells the protein is put in, the cells become light-sensitive.

This gives us a new perspective on how light controls neural activities, and how neural circuits govern specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders. In clinical medicine, optogenetics may be used in visual repair.

Literature

This award was given to Anne Carson. Her contribution to translating classical Greek is highly recognized, especially Sappho’s poem fragments, “If Not, Winter” (2002), along with tragedies such as Sophocles’s “Electra” (2001) and “Antigone” (2015), as well as Euripides’s “Bakkhai” (2015).

Her own poems vary across classical and modern forms and genres. Nobel Committee Chair Anders Olsson said: “Her collaborations with visual artists and choreographers and with opera and theatre directors demonstrate the freedom with which she relates to literary expectations and rule systems. It is this that lies behind the outstanding importance her work since the 1990s has had for the international art and literature scene.”

Economic Science

This award was given to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford. They used microeconomics to show that economic models could be reconstructed to revitalize stabilization policies. Stabilization policies aim to manage economic growth in a steady way through the manipulation of fiscal measures like interest rates.

This model helped to comprehend the past theorems, which didn’t regard microeconomics as a crucial part in analyzing the macroeconomic pattern. A key foundation of their model is that households and businesses are forward-looking when deciding on savings or product prices. The model can be used for future policymaking. According to John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, “The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume.

Maxwell S. Wright:

Physics:

This award was given to Francis Halzen. Halzen studies neutrinos, which are extremely small particles, 8.5 times smaller than a hydrogen atom! Neutrinos are like neutrons in that they have no charge, but due to how small neutrinos are, they tend to pass through most things without affecting them, which makes it very difficult to detect their presence. Halzen proposed using ice at the South Pole to detect neutrinos. Although uncommon, on the occasion that a neutrino hits another particle, a very faint light is produced. In the IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole, there is an array of mirrors inside the ice that reflect this light towards detectors. Because Antarctica’s ice is untouched and very old, it is exceedingly clear, allowing the light from neutrino interactions to travel through it for miles to a place where it can be observed. Due to their high amounts of energy, researchers know that the neutrinos that Halzen’s experiment found are actually from distant galaxies. Further study of these neutrinos may provide insight into our understanding of black holes and other things well beyond our solar system.

Chemistry:

This award was given to Henri B. Kagan and Keno Soai. Their work involves the chirality of molecules. Molecules are chiral if they don’t look the same as their reflection in a mirror, like your right and left hands. For example, a water molecule will look the same as its reflection, but an ibuprofen molecule would not. So, chemists call the two variants of molecules that look like either side of the metaphorical mirror “left-handed” and “right-handed.” This is important because left and right-handed ibuprofen can have different effects on the body. In nature, molecules are strangely only found as either left-handed or right-handed and do not typically mix, a phenomenon known as homochirality.

The question of how homochirality begins has plagued chemists for over a century, but Kagan and Soai found a way of producing a chemical reaction that produces only one variant of the product molecules. This understanding can make the processes by which drugs, like ibuprofen, are produced more efficient.

Peace:

This award was given to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, a South African legal expert who has worked for the International Criminal Court and the United Nations in the past. During her time with the U.N., Pillay was the chair of the U.N. National Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, eventually determining that Israel has committed genocide in the Gaza Strip.

Pillay’s reception of this award has been controversial, with many in the public sphere disavowing her previous work. President Donald Trump has spoken out against the International Criminal Court and has urged several countries to leave it. Despite this, at her reception ceremony, Pillay joked that she would share her award with the president if her audience continued their applause.

The Nobel Committee notes on their website that “At a time when the number of wars and conflicts is rising, and when judges and institutions of international law are under political attack, the Nobel Committee wishes to issue a reminder that the ability to resolve conflicts without force or violence is dependent on the international rule of law. An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world.”
